scenarios.scenario: Quarterly security pass: about 400 route handler files each need the identical audit step for missing authorization checks, every finding must be adversarially verified before it is reported, and next quarter the whole pass should rerun the same way from a single command.

key.primary: Dynamic workflow: a script fans out one auditor subagent per file, a verifier stage cross-checks findings, and the run is saved to .claude/workflows/ as a reusable slash command
key.rejected_alternative: Spawning many parallel subagents directly from the main conversation
key.rejection_reason: The main agent coordinates subagents turn by turn and every result returns to its context window; at 400 items that exceeds what one conversation can coordinate (20 concurrent subagents and 200 per session by default), and the orchestration is not repeatable. The workflow runtime runs dozens to hundreds of agents per run (up to 1,000, 16 concurrent), keeps intermediate results in script variables instead of any context window, and a saved run reruns as /<name>. This is the docs' own 'audit many files for the same issue' shape.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (each spawned agent has its own context; intermediate results live in script variables, and only the final report reaches the session)
key.lifecycle: explicit invocation: 'use a workflow' or the ultracode keyword in a typed prompt, later the saved /<name> command; a launch approval prompt gates the run per permission mode
key.failure_mode: Stopping mid fan-out is expensive on resume: cached results stop at the first unfinished agent and every agent started after it reruns; exiting Claude Code forfeits resume entirely (resume works only within the same session); no mid-run user input is possible.
key.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans only; on Pro it must be enabled from the Dynamic workflows row in /config

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: a JavaScript orchestration script Claude writes that discovers the route handler files, fans one auditor subagent out per file with pipeline(), then runs an adversarial verification phase over the findings before anything is reported. Saved into .claude/workflows/ so the quarterly pass reruns as a single slash command.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Parallel subagents driven turn by turn from the main conversation. 400 identical audits plus a verification pass is far past what one conversation can coordinate, and the orchestration itself would not be a rerunnable artifact, only the worker definition would be.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude only authors the script; the workflow runtime executes it, so the per-file fan-out, the verification phase, and the ordering are enforced by code rather than by the model's turn-by-turn judgment.
sheets.context_boundary: Each auditor and each verifier runs in its own subagent context window. Intermediate findings live in script variables inside the isolated workflow runtime, and only the final filtered report crosses back into your session's context.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs when you invoke the saved command (or when a run is started with an ultracode / 'use a workflow' prompt). It stops when the script returns, when you stop it from /workflows, or when you exit Claude Code mid-run, in which case the next session starts it fresh rather than resuming.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly. The runtime takes no mid-run user input and caps concurrency and total agents, so a bad file slice or a stopped run under-reports rather than erroring. Stopping mid fan-out is expensive: on resume every agent that started after the first unfinished one runs again even if it had completed.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan (on Pro it must be switched on from the Dynamic workflows row in /config), or Anthropic API access or Bedrock / Google Cloud Agent Platform / Microsoft Foundry. Saving the script into a monorepo .claude/workflows/ needs v2.1.178 or later, and the symlink check on save needs v2.1.216.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow saved to .claude/workflows/, invoked as /<name>. The script fans one audit agent per route handler file with pipeline(), feeds each finding to a second adversarial verifier agent before it counts as reported, and returns the collected verified findings.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents delegated turn by turn from the main conversation. About 400 files plus a verifier per finding is more than one conversation can coordinate, and the orchestration itself would not survive as a rerunnable artifact for next quarter.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude authors the script once, but the workflow runtime executes the fan-out and the ordering, so the verification stage cannot be skipped for a given file by model judgment.
sheets.context_boundary: Every audit agent and every verifier runs in its own context window inside the workflow runtime, and the intermediate findings live in script variables. Only the value the script returns crosses into my conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs on explicit invocation, as the ultracode or use-a-workflow opt-in for the first pass and as the saved /<name> command for later quarters, and it stops when the script returns. It applies to nothing between invocations.
sheets.failure_mode: It fails incomplete rather than loudly. Resume is scoped to the session that launched the run, so exiting Claude Code partway through a 400 file pass throws the progress away and the next session restarts the whole pass.
sheets.version_caveat: Dynamic workflows need Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan; on Pro they must first be switched on from the Dynamic workflows row in /config, and an organization can remove them entirely with disableWorkflows in managed settings.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow (programmatic orchestration behind one slash command) that fans out one audit subagent per route file with bounded concurrency, then routes every candidate finding through a separate adversarial verifier subagent before it is allowed into the report. The workflow definition plus the auditor and verifier subagent definitions are checked into the repo (or shipped as a plugin), so next quarter is a single re-invocation of the same command.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An ad hoc subagent fan-out driven by the main agent from a skill: it performs the same 400 audits, but the file coverage, the concurrency cap, and the mandatory verification step are all instructions the model may reorder or skip, so the quarterly rerun is not reproducible.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness for the mechanics (which files get audited, and that no finding is emitted without passing the verifier step), model for the substance (whether an authorization gap is really present). The gate is only real if the orchestration code refuses to append an unverified finding rather than merely asking for verification.
sheets.context_boundary: Each file audit runs in its own subagent window holding that handler plus the audit rubric; each verification runs in a third window seeing the finding and the code but not the auditor's reasoning. Only structured findings cross back to the driver, so no single context ever holds 400 file bodies.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs on explicit invocation of the command, once per quarter, and ends when every file has been audited and every surviving finding verified. Nothing persists between quarters except the checked-in workflow and subagent definitions.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on recall: a subagent returning 'no findings' is indistinguishable from one that ran badly or errored, and per-file isolation hides authorization enforced in middleware or the router, so false negatives are silent. The adversarial verifier only suppresses false positives; nothing catches what was never proposed. At 400 units, unbounded fan-out also hits rate and concurrency limits, so a fixed worker pool is required.
sheets.version_caveat: In-product dynamic workflow orchestration is a recent Claude Code addition and I cannot state its minimum version, flag name, or whether it is still experimental from model knowledge alone. Subagents plus a slash command (or a headless CLI driver) are the version-safe fallback and need no gate.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow. Claude writes a JavaScript orchestration script that lists the route handler files, runs one audit agent per file with pipeline(), and then runs a second adversarial verification phase over each finding before it is reported. Save that run's script from /workflows with `s` into .claude/workflows/ so next quarter it reruns as a single /command, passing the target paths through the `args` global.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents fanned out from the conversation turn by turn. At 400 files Claude has to re-decide each batch, every agent result lands in the main context window, and the only repeatable artifact is the worker definition rather than the orchestration itself.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the saved script, so the per-file fan-out and the adversarial verification phase are code the runtime runs, not judgment Claude re-exercises each quarter. The model still owns what any individual audit agent concludes inside a phase.
sheets.context_boundary: The script runs in an isolated workflow runtime, separate from your conversation, and intermediate audit and verification results live in script variables. Each agent has its own context window; only the script's return value, the surviving findings, crosses into Claude's context.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs when you invoke the saved command, type the ultracode keyword, or ask for a workflow in your own words, and it stops when the script returns, when you press `x` in /workflows, or at the runtime's cap of 1,000 agents per run. A stopped run is resumable only within the same session; exiting Claude Code makes the next session start it fresh.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on quality: the verification phase filters findings but nothing blocks a wrong verdict, and the runtime accepts no mid-run user input, so a shell command or MCP call outside your allowlist stalls the run behind a permission prompt. Stopping mid fan-out is expensive because replay follows start order and every agent that started after the first unfinished one reruns.
sheets.version_caveat: Dynamic workflows require Claude Code v2.1.154 or later, are available on paid plans plus Anthropic API, Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry, and on Pro must be switched on in the Dynamic workflows row of /config. 400 files far exceeds the default `medium` size guideline (fewer than 15 agents, default since v2.1.219) and the 25-agent Large workflow warning added in v2.1.203, so raise workflowSizeGuideline; the symlink check that keeps the saved file where you chose needs v2.1.216.

scenarios.scenario: Run the strict type check, fix whatever it reports, run it again, and keep looping until it passes or two consecutive rounds make no progress. Nobody should babysit the loop or re-decide anything between rounds.

key.primary: Dynamic workflow: the script holds the check-fix-recheck loop and the deterministic two-rounds-no-progress termination condition
key.rejected_alternative: Chaining subagents turn by turn from the main conversation
key.rejection_reason: With chained subagents the model re-decides after every round and each round's results land in the main context, so a long loop both drifts (the stop condition is judgment, not code) and bloats context. The workflow docs give this exact prompt as a canonical shape ('keep fixing until a check passes... or two rounds in a row make no progress'): the script owns the iteration and the stop condition, and the session receives only the final outcome.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (per-round agents; loop state and round results held in script variables)
key.lifecycle: explicit invocation via the workflow request or ultracode keyword, or a saved command; approval prompt at launch
key.failure_mode: No mid-run user input, so if a fix genuinely needs a human call the run cannot pause to ask; a loop that stalls without triggering the stop condition burns agents toward the 1,000-agent per-run cap; exiting the session loses resumability.
key.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans; Pro enables via /config

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: the check / fix / recheck loop, the round counter and the two-consecutive-rounds-without-progress stop condition all live in the script body, with one agent per round doing the fixing.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill. A skill is instructions Claude follows in the main context, so the loop condition and the no-progress comparison get re-decided by the model every round, which is exactly the babysitting the request rules out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the script, and the script itself holds the loop and the branching, so termination is a coded condition rather than a judgment call Claude makes between rounds.
sheets.context_boundary: Each round's fixer runs as its own subagent; the error lists, the round counter and the progress comparison stay in script variables in the isolated runtime. Only the final outcome, passed or stalled, reaches your conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when you request the run (the ultracode keyword typed at the prompt, a natural-language 'use a workflow', or a saved command) and stops when the type check passes, when the no-progress condition trips, or when you stop it from /workflows.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and unattended. Nothing can interrupt the loop except an agent permission prompt, so a mis-specified progress metric keeps spending until the runtime's 1,000-agent-per-run cap stops it, and a fix that satisfies tsc by weakening types is never questioned because no human is in the loop by design.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan or API/Bedrock/Google Cloud Agent Platform/Microsoft Foundry access; on Pro it must be enabled from the Dynamic workflows row in /config. The ultracode keyword only opts in when you type it yourself: it is ignored from -p prompts, scheduled tasks and relayed webhook or PR comments from v2.1.210 onward.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow whose script holds the loop: run the strict type check, fan fixes out to agents, re-run, and terminate on a pass or on two consecutive rounds with no progress. The stopping rule is code, not a judgment call re-made each round.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that instructs Claude to iterate in the main conversation. The instructions are followed by the model turn by turn, so the termination condition is re-interpreted every round and the growing check output accumulates in the session context.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the branching and the loop counter, so the round count and the no-progress test are not the model's to reconsider.
sheets.context_boundary: The runtime executes the script separately from my conversation; each round's type-check output and each fix agent's work stay in that agent's window and in script variables. Only the final outcome returns.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts on one invocation, by including the ultracode keyword or asking for a workflow in my own words, and runs in the background until the script's own exit condition is met. It stops applying the moment the script returns.
sheets.failure_mode: It is closed to intervention, which is what I asked for and also the risk: nothing but an agent permission prompt can pause a run, so a loop that keeps making cosmetic progress cannot be redirected mid-flight and burns agents until it hits the runtime cap.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan, with a /config toggle on Pro. The workflowSizeGuideline setting, default medium since v2.1.219, also steers Claude toward fewer than 15 agents, which can under-size a long fix loop; it is advice, not a cap.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow. The check, fix and recheck loop plus the stop-after-two-rounds-without-progress rule live in the script's own JavaScript control flow, with an agent spawned per round to apply fixes, so the termination condition is executed code rather than a judgment call.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill. Skill instructions are followed by Claude in the main conversation, which means Claude rereads the loop condition and re-decides whether to continue on every round, which is exactly the babysitting and re-deciding the request rules out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the loop and evaluates the stopping condition; the model owns only what each fixing agent does inside a round.
sheets.context_boundary: The script runs in the isolated workflow runtime; each round's type-check output and the diffs live in script variables and in that round's agent context window. Only the final result, whether the check passed and what changed, crosses into your conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts on the ultracode keyword, an explicit request for a workflow, or a saved command, and ends when the type check passes, when two consecutive rounds make no progress, at the 1,000-agent cap, or when you stop it from /workflows.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on termination, because the stopping rule is real code, but open on quality: workflow agents always run in acceptEdits and inherit your allowlist regardless of your session's permission mode, so fixes are auto-applied unreviewed, and the runtime takes no mid-run input, so your only intervention is stopping the run.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan, with the Pro toggle in /config; /effort ultracode, which makes Claude reach for workflows unprompted, needs v2.1.203. A loop-shaped workflow is small so the default `medium` size guideline is not a constraint, but disableWorkflows in settings or managed settings, or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1, removes the mechanism entirely.

sheets.primary: A programmatic loop owned by code, either a dynamic workflow or a headless CLI/Agent SDK driver: the harness runs the strict type check, hands the error list to a fixer subagent, re-runs the check, and evaluates the exit predicate (zero errors, or two consecutive rounds with no reduction in the error count) itself.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill or slash command that instructs the model to loop. The stop decision then belongs to the model, which typically halts early, declares partial success, or re-litigates the approach each round, which is exactly the babysitting the request rules out. (A Stop hook that re-injects 'keep going' is the blunt cousin and lacks a progress predicate.)
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness. The round counter, the error-count comparison, and the exit condition are code; the model contributes only edits inside each round.
sheets.context_boundary: The driver holds counters and the current error list, nothing more. Each fix round runs in a fresh subagent window with just the current errors and the files it needs, which keeps a multi-round loop from accumulating the whole history in one context.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered on invocation, stops on a clean type check or when the no-progress predicate fires, and has no standing effect afterwards.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on liveness (it always terminates) but the quality gate is weak: the cheapest way to reduce an error count is casts, any, or suppression comments, so the loop can reach green while degrading the code. Harden the predicate with a no-new-suppressions check and a test run. Oscillation (fixing A reintroduces B) shows as a flat count and trips the no-progress exit instead of being diagnosed.
sheets.version_caveat: The shell or SDK form of this loop works today with no gate. The in-product dynamic workflow form is newer and I cannot state its version gate, flag, or experimental status from model knowledge alone.

scenarios.scenario: A review pass over recent changes should dispatch an independent verifier for each finding it produces, typically 5 to 10 findings, and none of the per-finding verification chatter should ever reach my conversation. I want exactly one final verified summary back.

key.primary: One subagent that spawns nested subagents: the reviewer delegates a verifier per finding and only the top-level summary returns to the session
key.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow with a review stage and a verify stage
key.rejection_reason: The fan-out is real but small and hangs entirely off one delegated task. The subagent docs name this exact shape as what nesting is for: 'a reviewer subagent that dispatches a verifier per finding, so the intermediate output never reaches your main conversation', with subagents able to spawn up to three layers below the main conversation by default. At 5 to 10 agents the workflow's launch approval, background runtime, and generated script buy nothing; workflows are for jobs that outgrow a handful of subagents.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (a nested subagent tree; intermediate results are confined to it and only the top-level summary returns)
key.lifecycle: model-decided delegation; nesting occurs inside the reviewer subagent when its tool list includes Agent and depth allows
key.failure_mode: At the depth limit the Agent tool is withheld and the leaf agent does the verification itself; verifier detail is only as visible as the reviewer's synthesis, so a weak summary hides verified evidence; every spawn counts against the 200-per-session subagent cap.
key.version_caveat: Nesting depth defaults to three layers as of v2.1.219, configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH (v2.1.217+); v2.1.217 to v2.1.218 defaulted to one layer, and v2.1.172 to v2.1.216 allowed five

sheets.primary: Nested subagents. Delegate the review to one reviewer subagent that keeps Agent in its tools list, and have it dispatch a verifier subagent per finding from inside its own context, so only the reviewer's single final summary returns to you.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow. It would also keep the verification traffic out of your context, but it adds a version and plan gate, a launch approval prompt, and a whole script for a job that is 5 to 10 verifications deep and fits comfortably inside one delegated agent.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Shared, and worth naming both halves: the harness enforces that a nested subagent's output stops at its parent and caps how deeply subagents nest, while the model owns whether the reviewer actually dispatches one verifier per finding and what survives into the summary.
sheets.context_boundary: Three levels: your conversation, the reviewer's context window, and one context window per verifier. Verifier reports cross only into the reviewer's window; the single boundary your conversation sees is the reviewer's final summary, which passes through subagent output scanning on the way in.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts when you delegate the review and ends when the reviewer returns its one summary. Every agent involved, reviewer and verifiers alike, counts against the 200-subagent session limit and the 20-concurrent limit, and 5 to 10 verifiers sit well under both.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails silently open on the depth limit: when nesting is capped at one layer the harness simply withholds the Agent tool from the reviewer, which then verifies its own findings in a single context and still hands you one confident summary, so the loss of independent verification is invisible in the output you receive.
sheets.version_caveat: The nesting default has moved repeatedly: v2.1.172 through v2.1.216 allowed five layers with no way to change it, v2.1.217 and v2.1.218 defaulted to one layer, which breaks this pattern outright, and v2.1.219 raised the default to three. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH (v2.1.217 or later) is how you set it, and the reviewer definition must not omit Agent from tools or list it in disallowedTools.

sheets.primary: Push the whole pass one level down: a dynamic workflow (or an Agent SDK / headless CLI driver) owns the review, dispatches an independent verifier per finding, merges the verdicts, and returns exactly one verified summary to your conversation.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Dispatching the verifiers directly from your session as subagents. Each verifier's return message lands in your transcript, so you receive five to ten partial reports instead of one, which is precisely what the request rules out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness owns the isolation and the single-message-out contract; the model owns whether an individual finding survives its verification.
sheets.context_boundary: The review runs in its own window; each verifier receives one finding plus the relevant code and not the reviewer's reasoning, which is what makes the verification independent rather than confirmatory. Only the merged summary crosses back to you.
sheets.lifecycle: Per review pass, on invocation; ends once every finding has a verdict and the single summary is emitted. Nothing persists afterwards.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open, and drops are silent: a verifier that cannot reproduce a finding kills a possibly true positive, and one merged summary hides that disagreement unless you require a per-finding verdict line with its evidence. The load-bearing detail is whether a subagent may itself spawn subagents; I cannot confirm the current nesting rule, and if nesting is disallowed the fan-out must live in a workflow or SDK driver rather than inside a single subagent.
sheets.version_caveat: Subagents are generally available with no flag. Subagent nesting depth and the availability gate for in-product dynamic workflows are exactly the points I cannot state from model knowledge; an Agent SDK or headless CLI driver is the version-safe way to get the single-summary guarantee today.

sheets.primary: Nested subagents: one top-level reviewer subagent that itself spawns a verifier subagent per finding and returns a single verified summary. The reviewer definition must keep the Agent tool so it can delegate the second layer.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow. It is the right shape at larger scale, but for 5 to 10 verifications the in-session nesting already keeps every intermediate result out of your window without the paid-plan and version gate or the per-run approval prompt.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split. The harness owns the cap: Claude Code allows nesting up to a set depth and withholds the Agent tool from a subagent at the limit. The model owns the behaviour: whether a verifier is actually dispatched per finding is the reviewer subagent's decision, driven by its prompt.
sheets.context_boundary: Findings and every verifier transcript stay inside the reviewer subagent's and the verifiers' own context windows. Only the top-level subagent's summary crosses into your conversation, so the per-finding chatter never reaches you.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when you delegate the review pass and ends when the top-level reviewer returns its summary; the verifiers end with it. The 200-subagents-per-session and 20-concurrent limits bound how many such passes and verifiers can run before the Agent tool starts failing.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed but degrades invisibly. At the depth limit the harness simply withholds the Agent tool, so the reviewer performs the verification itself and still returns one tidy summary, with nothing in the output telling you the independent verification never happened. Ten findings also mean ten agents against the concurrent and per-session caps.
sheets.version_caveat: The nesting default is version-dependent: five layers and unchangeable on v2.1.172 through v2.1.216, one (nesting effectively off) on v2.1.217 and v2.1.218, three from v2.1.219. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH exists only from v2.1.217, so on an older build you cannot raise or lower it.

sheets.primary: Nested subagents: one reviewer subagent that keeps the Agent tool in its tools list and dispatches a verifier subagent per finding, then returns a single verified summary. The documentation names this exact shape as what nesting is for.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow fanning verifiers out from a script. It would also keep the chatter out of my context, but it is the heavier mechanism for a five to ten item fan-out whose count is only known after the review runs, and it needs its own version and plan gate.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the containment: only the top-level subagent's summary comes back to me, whatever the nested layer produces. The model owns how many verifiers get dispatched and what survives into the summary.
sheets.context_boundary: Three layers of context. Each verifier has its own window and reports into the reviewer's window, the reviewer holds all the per-finding chatter, and only the reviewer's final summary crosses into my conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts when Claude delegates the review pass, the verifiers spawn inside that subagent and end when they report, and the whole thing stops when the reviewer returns its summary. Each invocation is a fresh instance.
sheets.failure_mode: It degrades invisibly. At the depth limit the Agent tool is withheld and the subagent at the limit does the verification itself and still returns one summary, so the output looks identical whether verification was independent or self-performed.
sheets.version_caveat: Nesting is gated on the spawn depth: by default a subagent can nest up to three layers below the main conversation, which is enough for reviewer plus verifiers. The default was raised to three at v2.1.219; v2.1.217 and v2.1.218 defaulted to one, which turns this pattern off, and CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to change it needs v2.1.217 or later.

scenarios.scenario: One engineer wants their personal habits (2-space indentation, conventional-commit messages, a preferred diff-review flow) applied in every repository they open on their machine, without pushing any of it onto teammates through shared repos.

key.primary: User-scope memory: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, optionally split into topic files under ~/.claude/rules/
key.rejected_alternative: A gitignored CLAUDE.local.md in each project
key.rejection_reason: CLAUDE.local.md is scoped to a single project, and because it is gitignored it exists only in the worktree where it was created. The user file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md loads automatically for all projects on the machine and is never shared through the repo.
key.lifecycle: Loaded at session start in every project; user scope loads before project scope, so project instructions appear later in context and win on conflict
key.failure_mode: Project-level instructions can silently override the personal preference where they conflict, and the file spends context tokens in every session whether relevant or not

sheets.primary: User-level memory: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on that engineer's machine, holding the indentation preference, the commit-message convention and the diff-review flow, paired with their personal ~/.claude/settings.json for anything that is configuration rather than instruction. User scope is per-machine and per-person by construction, so nothing reaches teammates.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A project CLAUDE.md, rejected because it is committed and would impose one engineer's personal habits on the whole team through the shared repo, which is exactly the outcome the request excludes.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness reliably loads the user memory file, but every item in it is a preference the model applies at its discretion.
sheets.context_boundary: Every session's main context window on that machine, in every repository they open. The file text crosses in at session start; nothing crosses into the repository or into a teammate's session.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies from session start in all projects on that machine, for as long as the file exists, and stops when it is edited or the engineer works on a different machine. It is not tied to any task or trigger.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and advisory, plus a precedence trap: when a personal preference collides with a project convention or a repository formatter config, project-scope instructions and the actual tooling win, so a 2-space preference will be silently overwritten by the repo's formatter. It also drifts as the file accumulates preferences nobody prunes.
sheets.version_caveat: User-scope ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is stable and requires no flag or plan. I would verify the current status of CLAUDE.local.md and of the import syntax against the installed version rather than trusting recall, since I believe the local-file variant has been superseded by imports but cannot state that with confidence.

sheets.primary: User-scope memory on that engineer's machine: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for the short habits, or split into topic files under ~/.claude/rules/ such as preferences.md and review-flow.md. Both load in every project opened on that machine and never enter any repository, so nothing reaches teammates.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.local.md at each project root. It is personal and gitignored, but it has to be created per repository and does not exist in other worktrees of the same repo, so it fails the 'every repository I open' half of the requirement.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. These are instructions delivered as context; the harness only decides which files load and in what order.
sheets.context_boundary: The main context of every session started on that machine, loaded before project-level CLAUDE.md and project rules, and also carried into non-fork subagents. Nothing about it crosses to teammates, and remote or cloud sessions do not read the local home directory.
sheets.lifecycle: Loads at every session start on that machine regardless of working directory. It stops applying if the engineer deletes the file, excludes 'user' from --setting-sources, or works in a session type that does not read their home directory.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory, fails open, and it tends to lose ties: project instructions are read after user instructions, so a repo that mandates 4-space indentation will usually win over the personal 2-space preference, and conflicts across levels are resolved arbitrarily rather than by an explicit behavioral precedence.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate. Worth knowing that imports inside user-scope memory files load without the external-import approval dialog that project-level external imports trigger, because user-scope files are treated as the engineer's own configuration.

sheets.primary: A user-scope instruction file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, optionally split into topic files under ~/.claude/rules/, carrying the 2-space indentation preference, the conventional-commit format, and the preferred diff-review flow. It lives on that engineer's machine only and is never committed to any repository.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A per-project CLAUDE.local.md. It also stays out of the shared repo, but it is per-repository and gitignored one repo at a time, so it would have to be re-created in every project instead of applying to every repository the engineer opens.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. User-scope instructions are the same advisory context as project instructions and differ only in scope and load order, so nothing in the harness makes a commit message come out conventional.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session context window on that one machine, loaded ahead of any project instructions. Nothing crosses into a teammate's context, because the file is never in source control and personal-scope imports are trusted without the shared-project dialog.
sheets.lifecycle: Loads at the start of every session in every project on that machine and applies for the whole session. It stops applying when the engineer edits the file, or simply by working on a different machine, since it is local configuration.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory, fails open, and it loses quietly: user scope loads before project scope, so a repository whose committed instructions say something different about indentation or commit format can win, and the model may pick one arbitrarily without flagging the conflict.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate, plan restriction, or experimental status applies to user-scope instruction files. The only enabling flag in this area is the opt-in interactive /init flow that can scaffold personal instruction files, which is off unless the environment variable is set.

sheets.primary: User-scope memory on that engineer's machine: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for the short preferences (2-space indent, conventional commits), with the longer diff-review flow split into ~/.claude/rules/ topic files. Nothing is committed anywhere.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A project CLAUDE.md in each repository. It would deliver the same instructions but is shared with the team through source control, which is the explicit constraint; the personal-but-project-scoped CLAUDE.local.md fails differently, needing one gitignored copy per repo and per worktree.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. These are personal instructions delivered as context, so Claude follows them by cooperation; nothing in the harness enforces two-space indentation or a commit message shape.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session context window of every session on that machine, loaded at launch before project-scope content, and re-sent to subagents that load the CLAUDE.md hierarchy. It is local to the machine, so cloud and Cowork sessions do not see it.
sheets.lifecycle: Loads at the start of every session in every project on that machine and lasts the session. It stops applying if the files are removed, or if the user scope is dropped from the settings sources at launch.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open, with a specific collision: user rules load first and project rules outrank them, so a repo that mandates 4-space indent wins, and where two instructions simply contradict, Claude may pick one arbitrarily rather than flagging the conflict.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate or plan restriction on user-scope memory. The relevant switch is the --setting-sources flag, which can exclude the user scope for a run, and the fact that remote or scheduled cloud sessions never read a local ~/.claude at all.

scenarios.scenario: We need Claude connected to an internal HTTP tool service that authenticates with short-lived tokens minted by our single-sign-on helper command. Tokens expire mid-session, and the service exposes no OAuth endpoints of its own.

key.primary: MCP server configured with headersHelper: a command that writes a JSON object of headers to stdout, run fresh at each connection and automatically re-run with one retry when a call returns 401 or 403
key.rejected_alternative: A static Authorization header in the server's .mcp.json entry using ${TOKEN} environment-variable expansion
key.rejection_reason: Environment expansion resolves once from the ambient environment, so an expired short-lived token leaves the connection failing until restart. The docs name headersHelper as the mechanism for authentication schemes other than OAuth, such as Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO, and Claude Code re-runs the helper, reconnects, and retries the call once on 401/403.
key.lifecycle: helper runs in a shell with a 10-second timeout at session start, on every reconnect, and on a 401/403 retry; there is no caching, so the script owns any token reuse
key.failure_mode: the helper executes arbitrary shell commands, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted; a helper that exceeds 10 seconds or prints non-JSON breaks the connection entirely
key.version_caveat: automatic helper re-run and single retry on 401/403 requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later

sheets.primary: An MCP server over the HTTP transport whose auth comes from headersHelper pointing at the SSO helper command: the helper writes a JSON object of header name and value pairs to stdout and Claude Code merges it into the connection headers. This is the documented path for schemes other than OAuth, including short-lived tokens and internal SSO.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A static headers.Authorization bearer token expanded from ${VAR} in .mcp.json. It loses because that value is resolved once when the config loads and cannot be re-minted, so the connection dies as soon as the token expires mid-session.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code executes the helper, merges its output into the headers, and on a 401 or 403 re-runs it, reconnects and retries the call once; the model neither sees nor manages the token.
sheets.context_boundary: The helper runs in a separate shell process from the session's working directory with its own environment (CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME, CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL, and CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT for plugin-provided servers). Only tool results cross into the session context; the minted token never does.
sheets.lifecycle: The helper runs fresh at each connection, meaning session start and every reconnect, with no caching, plus the automatic re-run when a call returns 401 or 403. It stops applying when the server entry is removed or the session ends.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. The helper gets a 10 second shell timeout, and a slow SSO call, a non-JSON stdout, or a helper that is not on PATH leaves the server unconnected while the session carries on without its tools. After the automatic retry also fails, the server is merely flagged as needing authentication in /mcp.
sheets.version_caveat: The automatic re-run of the helper on 401 or 403 requires v2.1.193. For a plugin-provided server, resolving a relative headersHelper path against the plugin root requires v2.1.195, and from v2.1.207 headersHelper no longer substitutes ${user_config.*} values; put those in headers or have the script read them itself.

sheets.primary: An MCP server entry of type `http` pointing at the internal service, with `headersHelper` set to the SSO helper command. Claude Code runs the command at connection time and merges the JSON object it prints on stdout into the connection headers, which is the documented path for authentication schemes that are not OAuth, specifically naming short-lived tokens and internal SSO.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A static `headers` block with environment-variable expansion, such as `"Authorization": "Bearer ${SSO_TOKEN}"` in `.mcp.json`. Expansion happens once when the configuration is read, so the token is frozen at whatever value the environment held at startup and the connection breaks the moment it expires mid-session, which is the exact failure the team described.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code executes the helper, applies its output as headers, and (from v2.1.193) re-runs it, reconnects, and retries once when a tool call returns 401 or 403. The model never sees or handles the token.
sheets.context_boundary: The token stays outside the model's context entirely. The helper runs as a shell subprocess with a 10-second timeout, from the session's current working directory, with `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME` and `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL` in its environment; only tool results cross into the conversation. If the server is plugin-provided, the helper also gets `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` and runs with its working directory set to the plugin root.
sheets.lifecycle: The helper runs fresh on each connection, meaning at session start and on every reconnect, plus on the automatic retry after a 401 or 403. There is no caching, so the script itself owns any token reuse. It stops applying when the server is removed, toggled off, or the plugin providing it is disabled.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed at the tool-call boundary but with a narrow recovery window: mid-session expiry is repaired only by the single 401/403 retry, and if that retry also fails the server is flagged as needing authentication in `/mcp` for the rest of the session and its tools go dark. Other real breakages are a helper that exceeds the 10-second timeout, one that prints anything other than a flat JSON object of string key-value pairs, and a relative script path that does not resolve from the session's working directory. Note also that `headersHelper` executes arbitrary shell, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted.
sheets.version_caveat: Automatic helper re-run plus reconnect and single retry on 401/403 requires v2.1.193 or later; before that an expired token simply broke the connection. For a plugin-provided helper, working-directory resolution at the plugin root and `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` substitution into `headersHelper` require v2.1.195. As of v2.1.207 a plugin `headersHelper` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` values because the command is shell-parsed; the server is reported as misconfigured instead, so have the script read the value from its own config file or environment.

sheets.primary: An MCP server entry using headersHelper: configure the internal service as an HTTP-transport MCP server and point headersHelper at the SSO helper command, which prints a JSON object of headers carrying a freshly minted bearer token.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A static headers.Authorization value expanded from an environment variable. It loses because the token is captured once at config load and expires mid-session with no mechanism to re-mint it.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code executes the helper, merges its stdout into the connection headers, and re-runs it on an auth failure; the model has no part in minting or refreshing the token.
sheets.context_boundary: The helper runs in a shell subprocess from the session working directory, or the plugin root for a plugin-provided server, and its output never enters the model's context. Only MCP tool results cross the boundary.
sheets.lifecycle: The helper runs fresh at every connection, meaning session start and each reconnect, with no caching, and again automatically when a call returns 401 or 403. It stops applying when the server entry is removed or the plugin providing it is disabled.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed with exactly one automatic retry: on 401 or 403 Claude Code re-runs the helper, reconnects with fresh headers, retries the call once, and only then marks the server as needing authentication. The helper has a 10 second shell timeout, so a slow SSO round trip breaks the connection instead of blocking.
sheets.version_caveat: Automatic helper re-run and single retry on 401 or 403 requires v2.1.193 or later. A plugin-provided relative headersHelper path resolving against the plugin root requires v2.1.195, and from v2.1.207 headersHelper no longer substitutes ${user_config.*} values.

sheets.primary: A locally launched stdio MCP server acting as an authenticating proxy in front of the internal HTTP service: on each request it shells out to the SSO helper command (or reads its cached token and re-mints when stale), attaches the bearer header, and forwards. Putting the credential logic in a process that runs per call is what survives mid-session expiry.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Configuring the internal service directly as an HTTP-transport MCP server with a static Authorization header interpolated from an environment variable. Rejected because the header is resolved once at connect time, so the connection dies the moment the short-lived token expires and only a session restart fixes it.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness spawns and supervises the proxy process, but the proxy itself owns the refresh contract. The model owns nothing here and should never see or handle the token.
sheets.context_boundary: The proxy is a separate operating-system process with no model context of its own; the SSO helper runs inside it. Only the tool schemas at connect time and the tool results cross into the session window, and the token must be kept out of both, including out of any error message the proxy returns.
sheets.lifecycle: The proxy starts when a session with the server configured begins and lives for the session; the token lifecycle is nested inside that, minted or refreshed on demand per call and discarded on process exit. It stops applying when the session ends or the server is removed from configuration.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed, which is the right direction: if the SSO helper cannot mint, the tool call errors and nothing happens. The practical problems are that the error surfaces to the model as an opaque tool failure, so it will retry the same call two or three times before reporting, and that if the proxy leaks the raw upstream 401 body it can put credential material into the transcript. A helper that opens an interactive browser or prompts on a terminal will hang the call, since the MCP process has no interactive console.
sheets.version_caveat: Environment-variable interpolation in MCP configuration exists in current versions, but I do not know of a native configuration field that runs a command to produce a header value per request, and I am not going to invent one. If such a field does exist in the installed version it would replace the proxy; absent that, the proxy is the mechanism that actually handles mid-session expiry.

scenarios.scenario: Two hours into a debugging session, I want to hand off drafting regression tests for the bug we just characterized. The helper needs all the accumulated findings, ruled-out hypotheses, config quirks, and stack traces from our discussion, and I do not want to re-explain any of it while I keep working on the fix.

key.primary: Conversation fork (/subtask, or the fork subagent type): it inherits the entire conversation history, system prompt, tools, and model, runs the side task in the background, and only its final result returns; it also reuses the parent's prompt cache.
key.rejected_alternative: Delegate to a named test-writer subagent with a delegation prompt summarizing the session.
key.rejection_reason: A named subagent starts from fresh context; the delegation message would have to compress two hours of nuance and would lose ruled-out hypotheses and quirks. The docs say to use a fork exactly when a named subagent would need too much background to be useful, and the fork's tool calls still stay out of the main context.
key.lifecycle: explicit /subtask <task> from the user, or Claude requesting the fork subagent type when fork mode is enabled
key.failure_mode: The fork inherits everything including wrong assumptions and context poisoning, so it gives no fresh perspective; it runs in the background by default, cannot spawn further forks, and steering it requires opening its transcript in the panel.
key.version_caveat: /subtask requires v2.1.212 or later (the command was /fork on v2.1.161 through v2.1.211); letting Claude spawn forks itself is experimental, controlled by CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT and a staged rollout

sheets.primary: A subagent invoked with an explicitly authored handoff brief: the main session serializes the findings, ruled-out hypotheses, config quirks and stack traces into the Task prompt, or writes them to a project file the agent is instructed to read first.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Assuming a fork or an inheriting helper would pick up the debugging history automatically, rejected because subagent context does not transfer implicitly and two hours of accumulated reasoning would be silently absent from the helper's window.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. Nothing in the harness checks that the brief is complete, so faithfulness of the handoff is entirely an authoring responsibility of the dispatching session.
sheets.context_boundary: The helper runs in a fresh context window containing only the brief plus whatever it reads itself; the drafted regression tests and a short report cross back. The debugging session keeps its own window for the fix work.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires once at handoff time and ends when the tests come back. If the fix work changes the diagnosis afterwards the brief is stale, and the helper has to be re-dispatched with an updated one rather than corrected in place.
sheets.failure_mode: Silent context loss: the helper re-derives or invents the parts of the picture the brief omitted and writes tests against a hypothesis you already ruled out. It fails open, because a thin brief produces confident wrong output rather than an error.
sheets.version_caveat: Whether the helper can genuinely run while you continue working in the same session depends on the installed version's background-task support for agents; I would not promise the parallelism without checking, and the handoff-brief pattern itself is version-independent.

sheets.primary: A conversation fork started with /subtask, for example /subtask draft regression tests for the bug we just characterized. The fork is a subagent seeded with the entire conversation so far, and it runs in the background while you keep working the fix in the main session.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A named subagent. It starts from a fresh context with only the delegation prompt, so the findings, ruled-out hypotheses, config quirks and stack traces would all have to be re-explained, which is the one thing ruled out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns what the fork starts with: it copies the parent conversation, system prompt, tools and model wholesale, so context transfer is not a model judgment. The quality of the drafted tests remains model-owned.
sheets.context_boundary: The fork gets its own window pre-loaded with the parent's full history and shares the parent's prompt cache. Its own tool calls stay out of your conversation; only the final result crosses back as a message.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts on the /subtask command, runs in the background until it returns its result into the main conversation, and can be steered or stopped from the panel below the prompt. It spends the session subagent budget and cannot spawn further forks.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory, with no enforcement anywhere: the fork inherits every wrong assumption accumulated over two hours along with the useful findings, and it pays for a full duplicate context window. Its result also lands back in the main conversation, so it is not free of context cost.
sheets.version_caveat: /subtask requires Claude Code v2.1.212 or later; on v2.1.161 through v2.1.211 the forked-subagent command was /fork. Claude spawning forks on its own is still experimental and subject to a staged rollout, controllable with CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT.

sheets.primary: A forked subagent started with /subtask, for example "/subtask draft regression tests for the bug we just characterized". A fork inherits the entire conversation so far instead of starting fresh, so every finding, ruled-out hypothesis, config quirk and stack trace is already in front of it.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A named subagent such as a test-writer definition. It starts from a fresh context with only Claude's delegation message, which is precisely the re-explaining you said you do not want to do.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness owns the handoff: it copies the conversation, system prompt, tools and model into the fork and runs it in the background. The model owns whether the resulting regression tests are any good.
sheets.context_boundary: The full message history crosses into the fork at spawn time. Its own tool calls stay out of your conversation and only the final result comes back, so your working context stays clean; because the system prompt and tool definitions are identical it also reuses the parent prompt cache.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when you run /subtask, runs in the background while you keep working on the fix, and ends when it posts its result into your conversation or you stop it with x in the panel. It is a snapshot: anything you and the main session discover after the fork spawned never reaches it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on staleness rather than blocking anything: the fork can drift from the live debugging session and draft tests against a characterization you have since revised. Its final output still lands in your main context, so a large test draft spends the context the fork was meant to protect, and a fork cannot spawn further forks.
sheets.version_caveat: /subtask requires Claude Code v2.1.212 or later; before that the forked-subagent command was /fork, default-on from v2.1.161. With agent view turned off, /subtask does not exist and /fork starts the forked subagent instead. CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=1 or 0 forces fork mode on or off; Claude spawning forks on its own is experimental. Forks count against the 200-subagents-per-session budget.

sheets.primary: A forked subagent started with /subtask, for example /subtask draft regression tests for the bug we just characterized. The fork inherits the entire debugging conversation and runs in the background while you stay on the fix.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A named custom test-writer subagent. It loses because a non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context and only the delegation prompt, so you or Claude would have to restate two hours of findings, ruled-out hypotheses and stack traces.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the handoff: it copies the conversation, system prompt, tools and model into the fork, so no re-explanation is needed. The model still owns whether the tests are any good.
sheets.context_boundary: The fork runs in its own window seeded with the full message history; its own tool calls stay out of your conversation and only its final result comes back as a message, so your main context stays clean.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts when you submit /subtask and runs in the background until it posts its result; you can open its transcript from the panel to steer it, stop it with x, and it counts against the session subagent budget.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open: the fork is a snapshot taken at spawn, so anything you discover in the main session afterwards never reaches it and it can drift from the current understanding of the bug. It also cannot spawn further forks.
sheets.version_caveat: The /subtask command requires Claude Code v2.1.212 or later; on v2.1.161 through v2.1.211 the command is /fork. Claude spawning forks on its own is experimental and subject to a staged rollout, which CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT set to 1 or 0 overrides.

scenarios.scenario: During coding sessions the assistant should look up and update tickets in our self-hosted tracker, which sits behind OAuth. Copy-pasting ticket text into the chat is exactly what we are trying to eliminate.

key.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added via claude mcp add / .mcp.json, exposing query and update tools with OAuth handled by the MCP authentication flow
key.rejected_alternative: A skill whose SKILL.md instructs Claude to call the tracker's REST API with bundled curl scripts
key.rejection_reason: The MCP docs describe exactly this trigger: 'Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat from another tool, like an issue tracker.' MCP gives typed tools, a managed OAuth flow, and per-tool permissioning; a script-based skill leaves credential storage, token refresh, and response parsing as hand-rolled shell plumbing.
key.enforcement_owner: split: the harness owns the client-side machinery, it runs the OAuth flow, stores and refreshes tokens, and evaluates per-tool mcp__ permission rules; the tracker service enforces access on its side by rejecting unauthorized requests with 401 or 403
key.lifecycle: Server connects at session start per its configured scope; the model calls its tools during turns subject to permission rules
key.failure_mode: Fails closed toward the tracker: on a 401 Claude Code refreshes the stored token, reconnects, and retries the request once, flagging the server in /mcp for re-authentication only if that retry also fails, so expired credentials pause tracker access until the user signs back in; a dropped HTTP connection is retried with exponential backoff up to five attempts before the server is marked failed; oversized ticket payloads are limited by the 25,000-token default MCP output cap (warning at 10,000).

sheets.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added with HTTP transport at project scope so the definition lives in a checked-in .mcp.json, and signed in through the /mcp panel's OAuth 2.0 flow. The server exposes read and update tools for tickets, so Claude calls them mid-task instead of anyone pasting ticket text.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that wraps curl or the tracker's CLI through Bash. It loses because the skill would have to carry and refresh the OAuth credential itself, has no typed tool surface for the model to discover, and gives no per-server connection, timeout, or re-authentication handling.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, and the split is the point: the harness owns the connection, the OAuth token store, the refresh and retry behaviour, and the permission gate on each MCP tool call, while the model owns whether and when to call a ticket tool at all. Availability is harness-guaranteed; use is not.
sheets.context_boundary: The server runs out of process, remote, in no context window of its own. Its tool schemas load into the main session context, and each call's result crosses back into that same context, capped by the MCP output limit. The coding session's conversation never goes to the tracker beyond the arguments of each call.
sheets.lifecycle: The server is configured once in .mcp.json, approved once per project, and connects at session start; it stays available for the session, reconnecting automatically on mid-session drops. It stops applying when the server is toggled off in /mcp, listed in disabledMcpServers, or the entry is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed at the tool boundary and advisory above it. If the OAuth token cannot be refreshed the server is flagged as needing authentication and its tools disappear; auth and not-found errors are not retried, so the run stalls until a human signs in again. The residual risk is the model routing around a missing tool by guessing ticket state from the repo instead of reporting the failure.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan restriction applies to self-hosted MCP servers. Version behaviour to note: transient refresh failures no longer sideline an OAuth server for the whole session as of v2.1.206, the startup notice listing servers that need sign-in requires v2.1.193 or later, and re-authenticate prompting on a rejected refresh token arrived in v2.1.195.

sheets.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added as a remote HTTP server (claude mcp add --transport http tracker <url>) at project scope so the .mcp.json is checked in and the whole team gets the same tools, with authentication handled by the server's OAuth 2.0 flow completed once from /mcp or claude mcp login. Claude then reads and updates tickets through purpose-built tools instead of prose pasted into chat.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that scripts curl calls against the tracker's REST API. It can carry the endpoint knowledge but has nowhere to hold an OAuth session, so it would push a bearer token into a file or an env var and re-implement refresh; MCP owns connection and auth, and a skill is the right layer only for teaching Claude the team's ticket conventions on top of it.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the connection, the OAuth token storage and the automatic refresh-and-retry on 401, and it owns permission prompts for the tools. The model owns the outcome that matters here, which is choosing to call the tracker tools rather than asking a human to paste ticket text.
sheets.context_boundary: The server's tool names load into the main session context at startup with full schemas deferred until a tool is used; ticket bodies and update results cross into the main window as tool results, one call at a time, instead of arriving as a pasted wall of text. With tool search enabled, tool definitions are fetched on demand rather than all being resident.
sheets.lifecycle: Connects at session start and reconnects automatically; the OAuth token refreshes silently and the server is flagged in /mcp only when a refresh also fails. It stops applying when the server is disabled or removed, when Clear authentication is used, or when a higher-precedence definition of the same name (local scope beats project beats user) shadows it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed and visibly: an expired or rejected refresh token means the tools are simply unavailable and Claude Code shows a startup notice pointing at /mcp, so the worst case is the team falling back to pasting, which is the outcome they were trying to eliminate. The sharp edge is non-interactive use: there is no /mcp panel in claude -p or the Agent SDK, so the OAuth flow cannot run there and someone must sign in from an interactive session first. A configured headers.Authorization that the server rejects reports a failed connection rather than falling back to OAuth.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan restriction. claude mcp login for signing in from the shell requires v2.1.186 or later, and its no-local-browser detection and --no-browser flag require v2.1.191; the reliable-refresh behaviour (a transient refresh failure no longer flags the server for the whole session) requires v2.1.206, and the startup notice v2.1.193. Project-scoped .mcp.json servers prompt for approval before first use, resettable with claude mcp reset-project-choices. A self-hosted server with a pre-registered redirect URI needs --callback-port, and restricted scopes may need --client-id with pre-configured credentials.

sheets.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, configured in the project's .mcp.json so every checkout gets it, exposing typed tools for ticket read and ticket update and handling the OAuth flow itself rather than through the chat. The model calls those tools during ordinary coding turns.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that wraps a curl or CLI script against the tracker API, rejected because it would force credential handling into shell invocations and gives no schema for the model to call against, whereas MCP is the mechanism designed for authenticated external systems.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Shared, and worth being precise about: the harness owns the connection, the OAuth handshake and the approval of the server, while the model owns the decision to call a tool and what to write back into a ticket.
sheets.context_boundary: The server runs out of process (local stdio or a remote HTTP endpoint); only the tool definitions are resident in the main session context and only tool call arguments and returned results cross the boundary. Credentials stay on the server side and never enter the transcript.
sheets.lifecycle: Connected at session start from the config file and available for the whole session. It stops when the session ends, when the server is disconnected, or when the OAuth token expires and re-authorisation has not been done, which in a non-interactive run means it simply is not available.
sheets.failure_mode: Two things bite in practice. Tool definitions from a broad server consume resident context in every session whether or not tickets are touched, and ticket bodies are untrusted text, so a hostile or careless ticket description is a prompt-injection vector straight into a coding session. It fails open in the useful sense: if the server is down the model degrades to asking for pasted text, which is the outcome the team wanted to eliminate.
sheets.version_caveat: Remote MCP servers with OAuth 2.0 authorisation require a reasonably recent Claude Code version, and project-scoped .mcp.json entries need per-user approval before the server is trusted; I cannot state the exact version at which OAuth-capable remote servers landed, so verify against the installed build.

sheets.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added as a remote HTTP server with `claude mcp add --transport http tracker <url>` at project scope so the `.mcp.json` entry is shared with the team, and authenticated through the OAuth flow from `/mcp` or `claude mcp login`.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A Skill wrapping the tracker's REST API through Bash and curl. It pushes token handling, pagination and error shapes into prose the model re-derives each turn, and it gives no managed credential store and no per-tool permission surface.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, with the harness owning the boundary. Claude Code owns the connection, the stored OAuth token and the approval prompt for a project-scoped server; the model owns the decision to call any given tracker tool.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session's context window, where MCP tools appear as ordinary tools. What crosses in is tool schemas, surfaced through tool search, and tool results; ticket text enters context only when a call returns it, and the credential never enters context at all.
sheets.lifecycle: Servers connect at session start, project-scoped ones after a one-time approval, and stay available for the session; a mid-session HTTP or SSE drop triggers automatic reconnection with backoff. It stops applying when the server is removed or disabled, or when its token can no longer be refreshed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open in the sense that the work quietly cannot be done: an expired token, a down server or schema drift leaves tools missing rather than blocking anything. The sharp edge is headless use, where there is no `/mcp` panel to complete the OAuth flow, so the tools stay unavailable until someone signs in from an interactive session.
sheets.version_caveat: OAuth works over HTTP and SSE transports but not WebSocket, which is header-only. Shell-side sign-in with `claude mcp login <name>` needs v2.1.186 or later, and before v2.1.206 a transient refresh failure wrongly flagged an OAuth server as needing authentication for the rest of the session.

scenarios.scenario: A CI job pipes each pull request diff to the assistant for a typo and lint pass. The output must be byte-for-byte reproducible no matter whose machine or which runner executes it; a teammate's personal automation or the project's tool-server config must not leak into the run.

key.primary: Headless invocation with bare mode: claude --bare -p with the prompt, --allowedTools for the needed tools, and any required context passed explicitly via flags
key.rejected_alternative: Plain claude -p in the CI script, reasoning that non-interactive mode is already isolated
key.rejection_reason: The headless docs state that without --bare, claude -p 'loads the same context an interactive session would,' including hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md from the working directory and ~/.claude. Bare mode exists precisely for 'CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine': a hook in a teammate's ~/.claude or a server in the project's .mcp.json never runs because bare mode never reads them.
key.lifecycle: Explicitly invoked per CI run as a one-shot non-interactive command; only flags passed on that invocation take effect
key.failure_mode: Fails closed by omission: bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, so any context or tool grant the CI run needs but the flags do not pass simply is not there, and the lint pass silently runs without it; a tool call outside --allowedTools also cannot be interactively approved mid-run, since handling permission prompts in non-interactive mode requires a --permission-prompt-tool handler.
key.version_caveat: --bare is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and is slated to become the default for -p in a future release; until then, omitting it changes behavior

sheets.primary: A non-interactive headless invocation (claude -p, or the Agent SDK wrapping it) from the existing CI job, with the environment pinned by flags rather than by whatever is on the runner: --strict-mcp-config passed without --mcp-config so no MCP servers load at all, --setting-sources restricted to project (or --settings pointing at a checked-in JSON file), and --bare or --safe-mode to skip auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins and CLAUDE.md. Add --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections so per-machine details (working directory, environment info, memory paths) move out of the system prompt, and --output-format json or --json-schema so the job parses a fixed shape.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Shipping the typo-and-lint pass as a project skill or plugin checked into the repo. It makes the instructions shared and versioned, but it does nothing about isolation: the run would still load the runner user's settings, hooks and .mcp.json alongside it, which is exactly the leakage being ruled out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, for the part that can be owned: the CLI flags decide deterministically what configuration is discovered and loaded, and no model decision affects that. Nobody owns byte-for-byte output equality, which is the part of the requirement that is not a configuration property.
sheets.context_boundary: One ephemeral headless context per pull request, inside the CI runner. The diff goes in as the prompt and the review comes out on stdout; with the isolation flags set, no user-level CLAUDE.md, hook output, skill description or MCP tool definition crosses into that window. Pair with --no-session-persistence so the run leaves nothing on disk to be resumed or reused.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the CI job invokes the command for a given diff and ends when the process exits; there is no session state, no resume, and nothing carried to the next pull request. It stops applying the moment the workflow stops passing the flags, which is why they belong in the checked-in workflow file rather than a developer's shell.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open in the direction that matters: forget --strict-mcp-config and the project's .mcp.json joins the run silently, and forget the setting-source restriction and a teammate's user-level hooks fire without any error to signal it, so the run still succeeds and just is not the run you specified. And the stated requirement is not fully achievable: these flags remove configuration variance, not model variance, so identical inputs can still produce different words. If byte-identical output is a hard requirement, the deterministic part has to be a linter and the model output has to be treated as advisory commentary.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan gate. --safe-mode requires v2.1.169 or later and, importantly, still applies managed settings policy including policy-configured hooks, status line and file-suggestion commands, so it is not total isolation on a managed machine; --bare differs by also relaxing permissions handling. --json-schema errors on an invalid schema only from v2.1.205 (before that it silently produced unstructured output), and --append-subagent-system-prompt requires v2.1.205. --tools does not affect MCP tools, so rely on --strict-mcp-config rather than a tool list to keep MCP out.

sheets.primary: A non-interactive headless invocation, claude -p (or the equivalent Agent SDK call) driven from the CI job, hardened for isolation: --bare to skip auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, --strict-mcp-config so only servers named on the command line load, an explicit --settings file plus a narrowed --setting-sources, a fixed --tools list, and the model pinned by full name rather than an alias. The diff arrives on stdin and the findings come back on stdout as JSON.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An in-repo skill invoked from an ordinary session on the runner. It loses because a normal session auto-discovers whatever is on that machine: the teammate's user settings, their personal hooks, their ~/.claude.json MCP servers, all of which change behaviour and are exactly the leakage the requirement rules out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Which configuration sources load is decided by Claude Code at startup from the flags, before the model exists; the model cannot re-enable a hook or an MCP server that was never discovered. What the model then reports about typos and lint is model-owned.
sheets.context_boundary: One short-lived process per CI run with a context built only from the flags and the piped diff. The diff crosses in, the review text crosses out, and nothing persists between runs; adding --no-session-persistence keeps the transcript off the runner's disk as well.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the CI job runs the command for a pull request, ends when the process exits and prints its result. There is no session to resume and nothing survives the job; the behaviour stops applying the moment the workflow step is changed.
sheets.failure_mode: Partial isolation, failing open toward the environment. Managed settings still take precedence over everything including command-line arguments, so a runner or an org policy file can inject hooks, permission rules, or MCP servers that --bare and --strict-mcp-config cannot exclude; environment variables and the runner's tool versions also differ. Beyond configuration, byte-for-byte identical prose across runs is not something any flag guarantees for a language model, so the check should assert on a normalised, machine-readable output shape rather than on an exact string.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan restriction on headless mode. Pin the model by its full name, because the short aliases resolve to the latest model and will silently move under you, which alone defeats byte-level reproducibility. Related gates: --safe-mode, the broader customization-off switch, requires v2.1.169 or later, --bg cannot be combined with -p from v2.1.198, and --strict-mcp-config does not filter servers passed inline via --agents or the SDK agents option.

sheets.primary: Claude Code in headless mode, invoked non-interactively from the CI job with the diff on stdin and an explicit isolated configuration: a settings file checked into the repo, a strict MCP configuration flag so only the declared servers load and none are inherited, an explicit tool allowlist, and a dated model snapshot rather than a floating alias. The isolation flags are the mechanism, not the prompt.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A GitHub Action using the default setup, rejected because a default run inherits whatever settings, plugins and MCP configuration the environment offers, which is exactly the leakage the team is trying to prevent.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Which configuration sources load is decided by the CLI flags and the environment, not by anything the model can be asked to do; the model owns only the review content.
sheets.context_boundary: A fresh single-purpose context per pull request, created and destroyed inside the runner. The diff and the fixed prompt cross inward; a structured result crosses outward to the job. No user-level settings, no personal automations and no session history are in scope.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs on each pull request event and ends when the process exits. Nothing persists between runs, which is a feature here: run N cannot be contaminated by run N minus one.
sheets.failure_mode: Be honest about the requirement: configuration isolation is achievable, but byte-for-byte identical output from a language model is not, because sampling is not guaranteed deterministic and a floating model alias silently changes underneath you.
