Treat reproducibility as hermetic inputs plus a pinned model snapshot, and if the pipeline needs exact bytes, make the deterministic part a real linter and use the assistant only for the judgement layer. Config leakage also fails open and silently, so assert in the job that no unexpected MCP server or settings file was loaded rather than assuming.
sheets.version_caveat: The strict MCP configuration flag and the settings-file override flag exist in recent versions but I cannot state their exact spelling or the version at which each landed, so read them off the installed CLI help before writing the job; separately, pinning to a dated model identifier rather than a family alias is required, since aliases are repointed over time and would break any reproducibility claim.

sheets.primary: A headless Agent SDK invocation, `claude -p` run by the CI job with the diff piped on stdin and the configuration pinned explicitly: `--strict-mcp-config` with no `--mcp-config` so no servers load, a restricted `--setting-sources`, the rules supplied from repo-checked-in files via `--settings` and `--system-prompt-file`, and `--output-format json` for a stable result shape.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A project Skill in `.claude/skills/` invoked by a plain `claude -p` run. It would be discovered alongside the runner's user settings, hooks, plugins and the project `.mcp.json`, which is the exact leakage this job must prevent.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The isolation comes from CLI flags Claude Code applies at startup, not from anything the model is asked to respect or remember.
sheets.context_boundary: One fresh, short-lived context window per CI run, inside the runner process. Only the piped diff and the explicit prompt and settings files cross in; nothing persists between runs because the process exits after the query.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the CI job runs the command against a pull request and ends when the process exits after printing its response. It stops applying the moment the workflow step finishes: there is no session to resume and no state carried to the next pull request.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on the leakage requirement if a flag is forgotten, since without `--strict-mcp-config` the runner's `.mcp.json` and user-scope servers load silently and the run still succeeds, just non-reproducibly. Managed policy settings are the residual leak, because even the strongest customization switch still applies policy-configured hooks and commands. Byte-for-byte identical output is also not something any flag guarantees: the flags remove configuration drift, not model nondeterminism.
sheets.version_caveat: The blanket switches are version-gated and not interchangeable: `--safe-mode` requires v2.1.169 or later and still applies managed settings policy, while `--bare` skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md but also strips the tool set down to Bash plus file read and edit. The explicit `--strict-mcp-config` and `--setting-sources` combination carries no version marker in the mirror.

scenarios.scenario: Compliance needs an accurate record of every shell command the agent actually executed on developer machines, captured automatically with the full command line, rather than relying on the model to self-report what it ran.

key.primary: PostToolUse hook with a Bash matcher whose command appends the executed command and its result from the hook's stdin JSON to an audit log
key.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook with a Bash matcher that logs each command
key.rejection_reason: PreToolUse fires before permission evaluation and before the call runs, so it records attempts that a deny rule, a hook, or the user subsequently blocked; the audit trail would contain commands that never executed. PostToolUse fires only after the tool call succeeds, and logging operations is one of its documented use cases.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the hook is a shell process that receives the executed command and its result as JSON on stdin); the audit trail flows outward to a log file on disk, and nothing returns to Claude's context from a logging hook that exits 0 quietly
key.lifecycle: PostToolUse event fires after each successful Bash tool call, receiving tool input and result on stdin
key.failure_mode: It captures successes only: commands that error need a companion PostToolUseFailure hook, and the log lives on each developer's machine unless the hook itself ships entries to central storage.

sheets.primary: A PostToolUse hook with matcher Bash (plus PowerShell on Windows), and the same handler wired to PostToolUseFailure, appending tool_input.command together with session_id, cwd, agent_id and a timestamp to an append only audit log shipped off the machine.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook. It records intent rather than execution: it fires before the permission decision, so commands that were denied, deferred or never run would appear in the compliance record as though they had executed.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code fires the event carrying the literal tool_input it executed, so the record never depends on the model reporting its own commands.
sheets.context_boundary: The handler runs in its own process, receiving the full command line and the tool_response on stdin and writing them to the log. Nothing needs to cross back into the model context, and the logger should return no output at all.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires immediately after each Bash call that completes successfully, in the main conversation and inside subagents, whose input carries agent_id and agent_type. It runs for as long as the hook is configured on the machine.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open as an audit control: a handler that errors produces a non-blocking hook error while the command has already run, so the log silently gains a hole and nothing halts the session. PostToolUse alone also omits commands that ran and failed, which is why PostToolUseFailure has to be wired in as well.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on PostToolUse. On Windows shell work can arrive through the separate PowerShell tool surface, associated with CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL, so a Bash only matcher can miss calls. Hook stdout is capped at 10,000 characters, so the handler must write to the log file rather than to stdout.

sheets.primary: A PostToolUse hook with matcher Bash that appends .tool_input.command together with session_id, cwd, and timestamp to an append-only audit log or ships it to a collector, paired with a PostToolUseFailure hook on Bash so commands that errored are recorded too. Deploy it through managed settings with allowManagedHooksOnly set to true so a developer cannot unregister it.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook on Bash. It records intent rather than execution: a command a deny rule or another hook blocks never ran, so the log would over-report and fail the "actually executed" requirement.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code writes the record from its own tool-execution path, so the log does not depend on the model self-reporting what it ran.
sheets.context_boundary: A separate process outside the conversation. The full event JSON crosses in on stdin, including tool_name, tool_input.command, tool_response, duration_ms, session_id, cwd, and agent_id/agent_type when the call came from a subagent. Nothing needs to cross back into the model's context.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires immediately after each Bash tool call completes, in the main conversation and inside subagents, for every session on every machine that receives the managed policy. It stops when the managed policy is withdrawn.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open as a control and is incomplete by construction: PostToolUse cannot block, the command has already run, and a hook that errors just loses the entry while the turn continues. Coverage is limited to what went through the Bash tool, so commands a script the agent launched then executed internally never appear, and PostToolUse alone would silently omit failed commands.
sheets.version_caveat: allowManagedHooksOnly is a managed-settings-only key and has no plan restriction. Hooks from plugins force-enabled in managed enabledPlugins remain exempt, so audit that allowlist too, and note that disableAllHooks cannot disable managed hooks from outside managed settings.

sheets.primary: A PostToolUse hook with matcher "Bash" (and "PowerShell" on Windows) that appends tool_input.command together with session_id, cwd, timestamp and the tool_response exit status to an append-only record, or a type: "http" hook that POSTs the same payload to a central collector. Deploy it through managed settings so it is present on every developer machine rather than opt-in.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse logging hook. It fires earlier and catches more, but it records attempted calls including ones that were then denied or never executed, which is the wrong evidentiary record when the requirement is what actually ran.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook fires on the CLI's own dispatch path whether or not the model cooperates or even mentions the command, which is precisely why it beats self-reporting.
sheets.context_boundary: Runs in a separate process (or a remote endpoint for the HTTP form) and receives tool_input, tool_response and duration_ms from the CLI. Nothing needs to cross back into the model's context: the hook exits 0 with no stdout, so the audit trail is invisible to the session it is auditing.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires after every successful tool call matching the matcher, for as long as the settings source that defines it is loaded. Add a PostToolUseFailure hook with the same matcher to also capture commands that started and then errored, otherwise failed executions leave no record.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open as a control: it records what Claude Code dispatched, not what the shell ultimately did, so a single command that invokes a script, bash -c, a Makefile target or a background job hides the real work behind one log line. A local log file is also writable by the very developer being audited, and a hook that crashes does not stop the command. Ship to a remote collector and lock the hook down if the record has to hold up.
sheets.version_caveat: allowManagedHooksOnly is managed-settings-only and is what stops a developer's own settings from replacing or shadowing the audit hook; note also that disableAllHooks in a user settings file does not disable managed hooks unless it is set in managed settings too. HTTP hook destinations can be pinned with allowedHttpHookUrls and their env interpolation with httpHookAllowedEnvVars. On Windows set "shell": "powershell" on the hook command.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that appends the full command line, timestamp, session id, cwd and user to an append-only audit sink, paired with a PostToolUse hook on Bash to record the outcome, and shipped through managed settings so it is present on every machine rather than opted into per repo.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Parsing the session transcript files after the fact, which is accurate about what the model emitted but is local, deletable, format-unstable, and gives no real-time record.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The whole point of the scenario is that the model's self-report is not evidence, so the capture must sit in the tool-invocation path.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs outside the model context and receives the tool input JSON on stdin; nothing needs to cross back, so it should exit zero and stay silent to avoid polluting the transcript or slowing the turn.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on each Bash tool call for the life of every session on the managed fleet; the record stops the moment hooks are disabled or the agent is run through an install that does not read the managed config.
sheets.failure_mode: It records the command the agent asked for, not everything that executed: child processes, a script's internal calls, and anything run inside an interactive shell or a container are invisible. PreToolUse alone also logs intent, so denied or failed commands appear as if run unless the post-hook records status. A local log file is tamperable, so ship it off-box; and if the sink is unreachable the hook must not block, which means it fails open on the logging path.
sheets.version_caveat: The hook input schema (the field carrying the command text under the tool input object) and the availability of a separate telemetry / OpenTelemetry export path are both version-dependent, and telemetry may additionally be plan-gated. I cannot confirm the current field names or gating without the documentation, so validate the captured payload on the installed version.

scenarios.scenario: We want to shut off the entire aws CLI surface for the agent except one approved read-only invocation, aws s3 ls, which should go through without prompting. Every other aws command must be refused outright.

key.primary: PreToolUse hook on Bash that inspects the command and returns permissionDecision "deny" for aws commands unless they match the approved invocation (returning "allow" for that one)
key.rejected_alternative: permissions.deny Bash(aws *) paired with permissions.allow Bash(aws s3 ls)
key.rejection_reason: Rules evaluate in fixed deny, then ask, then allow order and the first match wins; rule specificity does not change the order. The permissions docs state a broad deny like Bash(aws *) blocks every matching call including ones a narrower allow also matches, so a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions. Exception logic must live in a PreToolUse hook, which the docs recommend for exactly this allow-everything-except pattern, and no deny rule for aws may remain in settings since deny rules override hook allow decisions.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the script runs as a shell process before each Bash tool call reaches execution); on a deny decision the reason crosses into the main conversation and is shown to Claude, while on an allow decision the reason is shown to the user but not Claude and the call simply proceeds
key.lifecycle: PreToolUse event fires before each Bash tool call, ahead of permission rules and any prompt
key.failure_mode: The hook script must handle compound commands itself: a naive check passes 'aws s3 ls && aws iam delete-user', and the protection exists only on machines where the hook is configured.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that parses the command and returns hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision "allow" for exactly an aws s3 ls invocation and "deny" for every other command whose executable is aws. A hook is required rather than optional here because deny rules cannot carry an allowlist exception.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A settings pair of permissions.deny ["Bash(aws *)"] plus permissions.allow ["Bash(aws s3 ls*)"]. The documentation uses this exact pair as its counter-example: rules run deny first and specificity does not reorder them, so the broad deny swallows the narrow allow and the approved read-only call would be refused along with everything else.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook is a harness-run script whose decision the permission layer applies, and a blocking hook takes precedence over allow rules, so the outcome does not rest on the model's judgement.
sheets.context_boundary: A separate process; tool_input.command crosses in on stdin and the decision plus permissionDecisionReason crosses back. The deny reason is shown to Claude so it can adapt, the allow reason only to the user. No conversation context is consumed.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on every Bash tool call before the permission prompt, in the main agent and in subagents, for as long as the hook is registered. It never fires for EndConversation, and it cannot see an aws call made from inside a script the agent already launched.
sheets.failure_mode: The deny half fails open if the script is fragile: Claude Code treats exit code 1 as a non-blocking error and lets the call through, so the refusal must be exit 2 or an explicit JSON "deny", and a missing jq or interpreter is a silent hole. Naive string matching is the other hole, since aws s3 ls && aws s3 rm ..., a leading variable assignment, or a wrapper can smuggle a second aws invocation past a prefix test.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate, plan restriction, or experimental flag applies. Write the decision as hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision with permissionDecisionReason; the older top-level decision field with "approve" and "block" is deprecated for PreToolUse and only maps onto the current values for compatibility.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook on Bash implementing an explicit allowlist: normalise the command, and if it is exactly an aws s3 ls invocation return an allow decision so it runs without a prompt, otherwise, for anything else touching aws, return deny with a reason.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Settings permission rules alone (allow Bash(aws s3 ls:*) plus deny Bash(aws:*)), which does not express this shape because deny takes precedence over allow, so the broad deny would also swallow the one command you meant to permit.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Both halves, the silent pass and the hard refusal, are decided outside the model.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook sees only the candidate command string; the allow or deny plus reason crosses back, and on deny the model gets the refusal text rather than any aws output.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs before every Bash tool call for the whole session; it stops applying if the hook is removed or if the agent reaches AWS by some route that is not the Bash tool, such as an MCP server or a Python SDK call.
sheets.failure_mode: Shell composition is the hole: pipes, command substitution, sh -c, a wrapper script, an alias, or an env-var-built command can carry an aws call the matcher does not recognise. Default the hook to deny whenever the command mentions aws and does not exactly match the approved form, so it fails closed and the cost is false refusals rather than silent escapes. Note also that boto3 or an AWS MCP server bypasses the Bash surface entirely.
sheets.version_caveat: A PreToolUse hook returning an allow decision that suppresses the permission prompt is a structured-output capability that older versions did not have (they only offered exit-code blocking), and the precedence rule that deny beats allow in the settings permission layer is what forces the hook design here. I cannot cite the introducing version, so confirm the allow decision actually suppresses the prompt on the installed build.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that parses tool_input.command and returns permissionDecision "deny" for every aws invocation that is not the approved read-only form, combined with an allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls) (plus Bash(aws s3 ls *) if arguments are wanted) so the approved call runs with no prompt. Narrow the hook with "if": "Bash(aws *)" so the process only spawns for aws commands.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A deny rule Bash(aws *) paired with an allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls). The docs are explicit that deny is evaluated first and rule specificity does not change the order, so the broad deny would block the approved call as well: a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness on both halves. The hook decision and the allow rule are both evaluated by Claude Code before the command executes, and PreToolUse fires ahead of the permission-mode check in every mode, including bypassPermissions and dontAsk.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs in its own process with only the command string handed to it; the deny reason string is the sole thing that crosses back into the model's context, where it becomes the tool error the model reads and adjusts to.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs before every Bash tool call for the whole session and reloads with the settings file. It applies to any session that loads the hook, so deploy it in managed settings if the shutoff must hold on machines whose owners would rather it did not.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed only if the script is written default-deny and exits 2 on its own internal errors; any other non-zero exit is treated as a hook error and the command proceeds, which is a fail-open path a naive script walks straight into. Command-string matching is the real weakness: compound commands, leading env assignments, wrapper runners, bash -c, a profile flag before the subcommand, or a Python boto3 script all evade it, and the allow rule's word boundary means aws s3 ls matches while a double-spaced variant does not.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on PreToolUse deny decisions or on Bash allow rules. The "if" filter is best-effort and fails open by running the hook when a command cannot be parsed, which is the safe direction here since the hook is the deny side. If the aws surface has to be genuinely closed rather than pattern-matched, move the boundary to credentials and network (sandbox credentials.envVars deny on AWS variables, or IAM) rather than to string matching.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that parses each subcommand and returns permissionDecision "deny" for every aws invocation that is not exactly aws s3 ls, paired with an allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls:*) in settings so the one approved call runs without a prompt.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A deny plus allow permission rule pair. Rejected on the first axis that settled it: deny is evaluated before allow, so a broad Bash(aws *) deny also blocks the narrower Bash(aws s3 ls) allow, and a deny rule cannot carry an allowlist exception.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. PreToolUse hooks run before the permission prompt and a hook deny blocks the tool even under bypassPermissions or --dangerously-skip-permissions, so the model cannot argue past it.
sheets.context_boundary: The decision is made in the hook process from tool_input.command, outside the context window. Only permissionDecisionReason crosses back to the model on a deny, which is what lets it stop retrying variants.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs after Claude creates the tool parameters and before the call is processed, on every Bash call for the session. It stops applying if the hook entry is removed, or if hooks are disabled at the same or a higher settings tier.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on handler error, because any exit code other than 2 is a non-blocking error and the command proceeds. The fragile part is the matching: compound commands, environment runners such as devbox run or docker exec, and aws called from inside a script can evade a prefix test, so parse subcommands rather than string matching, and do not lean on the if filter, which is best effort and itself fails open.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate is documented in the mirror for PreToolUse allow and deny. The binding constraint is directional instead: a hook can tighten but not loosen, so the hook can deny every other aws command, but its allow will not override a settings deny rule that also matches aws s3 ls.
